analysis.investment_thesis: Puravankara is a highly leveraged Indian real estate developer where finance costs of ₹555 Cr in FY25 exceed operating income of ₹291 Cr, producing a ₹183 Cr net loss and negative free cash flow of -₹572 Cr. With a D/E of 2.75, shrinking equity, and only 2.7% revenue CAGR over nine years, this is a capital-intensive, cyclical business with no discernible moat — precisely the kind I avoid.
key_strengths: High promoter ownership at 75% signals skin in the game
Gross margins of 44% and operating margins of ~19% indicate decent project-level economics
FII ownership at 16.7% shows institutional interest and reasonable liquidity
key_risks: Debt burden is existential: borrowings surged to ₹4,497 Cr in FY25 from ₹2,670 Cr in FY20 while equity eroded from ₹1,914 Cr to ₹1,619 Cr
Finance costs (₹555 Cr FY25) growing at 9.6% CAGR far outpace revenue growth of 2.7%, making profitability structurally improbable
Operating cash flow swung to -₹531 Cr in FY25 from +₹896 Cr in FY24 — extreme volatility signals project-completion lumpiness and execution risk
red_flags: ROE of -10% and net loss of ₹183 Cr in FY25 — equity is being consumed
Finance costs exceed operating income in FY25 (₹555 Cr vs. ₹291 Cr), meaning operations cannot service debt from earnings
Free cash flow deeply negative at -₹572 Cr in FY25 after a decade of erratic, mostly thin positive FCF
Total assets grew 90% (₹8,071→₹15,335 Cr) since 2020 funded almost entirely by debt, not retained earnings
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Puravankara embodies every characteristic I instinctively avoid. Real estate development is capital-intensive, cyclical, and commoditized — there is no brand moat, no switching cost, no network effect. Revenue has compounded at a mere 2.7% over nine years, barely keeping pace with inflation, while debt has grown 68% since FY20. The company earns a ROCE of just 6% — below any reasonable cost of capital — meaning every rupee reinvested destroys value. The P/B of 3.3x for a loss-making, over-leveraged developer trading at EV/EBITDA of 21x is not a bargain; it is a value trap.

The FY25 numbers are alarming in their deterioration. Finance costs of ₹555 Cr consumed not just profits but operating income itself, explaining the ₹183 Cr net loss. Operating cash flow collapsed to -₹531 Cr from +₹896 Cr just one year prior, and the company had to raise ₹354 Cr in net financing to stay afloat. When a business must borrow to fund operations, the equity holder is subordinated to creditors. At Berkshire, I would not touch this business at any price without a dramatic deleveraging, demonstrated earnings recovery, and a price closer to distressed-asset levels — none of which apply at ₹225/share.
